say.text: Welcome to class 54: World War II. Today we outline where it was fought, and how it ended.

show.text: World War II: the main fronts and the ending

say.text: First, one word. A 'theater' is a large region where a war is fought. This war had two main ones: Europe and the Pacific.

show.text: Theater = a large region of fighting

ask.q: In war language, what is a 'theater'?
ask.right: A large region where a war is fought
wrong: A building where plays are shown
ask.why: A theater is a large region of fighting. The European theater and the Pacific War were the two main ones.

say.text: Most histories count the war as six years long, from 1939 to 1945.

show.text: 1 Sep 1939 Germany invades Poland | 1940 France falls | 1941 Germany attacks USSR; Pearl Harbor | 1944 D-Day | 8 May 1945 war ends in Europe | 2 Sep 1945 formal Japanese surrender

say.text: We'll go region by region, starting with Europe. On 1 September 1939, Germany invaded Poland.

show.text: Map of Europe: arrow from Germany into western Poland, marked 1 Sep 1939

say.text: Two days later, Britain and France declared war on Germany. On 17 September the Soviet Union invaded Poland from the east, and the two powers divided it between them.

show.text: Same map: second arrow from the east, 17 Sep 1939. Poland split in two.

ask.q: Which two countries declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939?
ask.why: Britain and France declared war on 3 September 1939, honoring their promise to protect Poland's borders.

say.text: Germany fought with 'blitzkrieg', which means 'lightning war': a swift, hard-hitting attack.

show.text: Blitzkrieg = lightning war

ask.why: Blitzkrieg means 'lightning war'. Germany opened the war in Europe with swift, brutal attacks.

say.text: In 1940 the tide of conquest rolled west. France signed an armistice with Germany on 22 June 1940.

show.text: A map of western Europe shaded in German-held colors, June 1940

say.text: Britain stood on. In the Battle of Britain, July to September 1940, the Royal Air Force beat the German air force.

show.text: Battle of Britain, July–September 1940

say.text: In June 1941, Germany attacked the Soviet Union. This opened the Soviet front, also called the Eastern Front.

show.text: Eastern Front = Germany vs the Soviet Union

say.text: This front was enormous. The historian Geoffrey Roberts says more than 80 percent of all combat in the war took place there.

show.text: 80%+ of all combat (Roberts's estimate)

say.text: At first the German invasion went very well. By September 1941 the Red Army had lost about 2.5 million men, and Germany besieged Leningrad to starve its people.

show.text: By Sept 1941: about 2.5 million Red Army casualties | Leningrad besieged and starved

say.text: The turning point came at Stalingrad. It was a five-month battle, and in February 1943 the trapped German forces surrendered.

show.text: Map of southern USSR with Stalingrad on the Volga marked; arrows closing around it

say.text: The cost was huge. Estimates vary: Britannica gives about 800,000 Axis and 1.1 million Soviet casualties, plus about 40,000 civilians.

show.text: Battle of Stalingrad: estimated casualties

ask.q: Why is Stalingrad called a turning point?
ask.right: After it, the momentum on the Eastern Front shifted to the Soviets
wrong: It was the last battle of the war
It was where the United States joined the war
ask.why: After the German surrender at Stalingrad in February 1943, the momentum on the Eastern Front had shifted.

say.text: Now to the sea. Britain needed supplies and troops shipped across the Atlantic, and German submarines called U-boats tried to cut that lifeline.

show.text: The Atlantic: a lifeline under attack

say.text: The Allies grouped merchant ships into convoys with warship escorts. The first convoy sailed on 2 September 1939, and the Battle of the Atlantic was the longest campaign of the war.

show.text: Convoy = merchant ships sailing together with escorts

say.text: U-boats answered with 'wolf packs': groups that attacked convoys together, usually at night. In convoy SC 7 in October 1940, 20 of 35 cargo ships were sunk.

show.text: 20 of the 35 cargo ships in convoy SC 7 were sunk

ask.right: A group of U-boats that attack a convoy together
ask.why: Wolf packs were groups of U-boats, often six or more, that attacked convoys together at night.

say.text: The worst month was March 1943, when U-boats sank 108 Allied ships. Then the tide turned. Long-range aircraft and new escort groups arrived, and in May 1943 the U-boats were beaten back.

show.text: 108 ships sunk in March 1943

say.text: Admiral Dönitz, who led the U-boats, admitted the result privately.

show.text: 'We had lost the Battle of the Atlantic.' (Admiral Karl Dönitz, privately, as reported by Warfare History Network)

ask.q: What helped turn the Battle of the Atlantic in 1943?
ask.right: Long-range aircraft and extra escort groups protecting the convoys
wrong: The U-boats ran out of torpedoes
ask.why: Long-range aircraft and support groups gave convoys far better protection. In May 1943 the U-boats lost heavily.

say.text: Back on land. On 6 June 1944, D-Day, American, British and Canadian troops landed in Normandy, in occupied France.

show.text: Map of the Normandy coast with five landing beaches, 6 June 1944

say.text: Now Germany was squeezed from both sides. In January 1945 Soviet forces freed Warsaw and Krakow, and on 21 April they entered Berlin.

show.text: Europe map: arrows from the west and from the east closing on Berlin

say.text: Germany surrendered unconditionally on 7 May 1945. The surrender took effect on 8 May, called V-E Day, Victory in Europe. Because of the time difference, the Soviets marked Victory Day on 9 May.

show.text: 7 May 1945 surrender signed | 8 May V-E Day | 9 May Soviet Victory Day

ask.q: Why did Soviet forces announce their Victory Day on 9 May?
ask.right: Because of the time difference, the surrender reached them on 9 May
wrong: They surrendered a day later than Germany
They were fighting a different war
They did not sign the surrender
ask.why: The time difference put the end of the fighting on 9 May for Soviet forces. Most of Europe marked it on 8 May.

say.text: Now Asia. The National WWII Museum says the war began on 7 July 1937, in China, when Japanese and Chinese troops clashed near Beijing.

show.text: Map of East Asia: clash near Beijing, 7 July 1937; Japanese advance to Nanjing

say.text: On 7 December 1941, Japan attacked the US naval base at Pearl Harbor in Hawaii. Japan also overran Allied lands in south-east Asia and the Philippines.

show.text: Pacific map: Pearl Harbor, the Philippines, Malaya

say.text: Days later, Germany and Italy declared war on the United States. America found itself in a global war.

show.text: Global war

ask.q: After Germany and Italy declared war on the US, what did America find itself in?
wrong: A war only in the Pacific
ask.why: Germany and Italy declared war on the US days after Pearl Harbor, so America faced enemies in Europe and the Pacific.

say.text: In June 1942 came the Battle of Midway. American carrier aircraft destroyed four Japanese aircraft carriers. It was a turning point, and the US could now go on the attack.

show.text: Midway, June 1942: four Japanese carriers destroyed

ask.q: Which June 1942 naval battle was a turning point in the Pacific?
ask.why: At Midway, US aircraft destroyed four Japanese carriers. That shifted naval power and let the US attack.

say.text: By 1945 Japan was squeezed. A firebombing of Tokyo on 9 to 10 March killed some 80,000 civilians. In April, American forces landed on Okinawa, only 350 miles from Japan.

show.text: March 1945: Tokyo firebombing, about 80,000 civilians killed | April 1945: Okinawa landings, kamikaze attacks | Bombing and a submarine blockade

say.text: Now a different question. What was life like away from the fighting? In 'total war', whole societies join in: factories, farms and families.

show.text: Total war = whole societies join the war effort

say.text: Governments handled new problems: rationing, who works where, defending the home, and moving people away from air raids.

show.text: Rationing | Shifting workers | Home defense | Evacuation from air raids

say.text: Britain brought in rationing in 1940. Every man, woman and child got a ration book. Men aged 18 to 41 were needed in the forces, so women took jobs in factories and on farms.

show.text: A British ration book beside a poster urging women to work in factories

say.text: In the United States, food, gas and clothing were rationed. Families planted 'victory gardens' to grow their own food. Women and African Americans took defense-plant jobs.

show.text: A family working in a backyard victory garden

ask.right: A home garden grown to add to rationed food
wrong: A prize for winning a battle
ask.why: Americans grew their own food in victory gardens as an alternative to rationing.

say.text: People often say the war was the first time American women worked for pay. That's a myth. About a quarter already did in 1940, but five million more joined the workforce by 1945.

show.text: 1940: about a quarter of women worked | 1940–1945: five million more joined

say.text: The Soviet Union mobilized millions of people, rationed goods, evacuated people and ran heavy propaganda. Women filled many jobs left by men at the front.

show.text: Mass mobilization | Rationing | Evacuation | Propaganda | Women replacing men

say.text: Under occupation there was another kind of home front: resistance. It ranged from refusing to cooperate, to spreading news, to hiding crashed pilots, to open fighting.

show.text: Resistance = opposing occupation, from quiet refusal to fighting

say.text: Danish resistance sabotaged rail lines. In February 1941 the Dutch held a general strike over the arrests and brutal treatment of Jews. In Germany, students in the White Rose group spoke out.

show.text: Denmark: sabotage | Netherlands: general strike, Feb 1941 | Germany: the White Rose, Hans and Sophie Scholl

ask.q: In February 1941, how did the Dutch protest the arrests of Jews?
ask.why: Called by the banned Communist Party with union activists, the Dutch held a general strike in February 1941.

say.text: Jewish people resisted too. Armed resistance arose in over 100 ghettos in occupied Poland and the Soviet Union. Elsewhere it often meant aid and rescue. The Holocaust has its own class next.

show.text: Armed resistance: over 100 ghettos | Aid and rescue: many countries

say.text: Resistance was dangerous. At Ploetzensee prison the Nazis executed hundreds of Germans for opposing Hitler. Overall, resistance is judged more by its moral and political impact than by military results.

show.text: Ploetzensee prison entrance, Berlin, a memorial to those executed

say.text: Now the end of the war in Asia. By summer 1945 Japan was bombed and blockaded. On 6 August 1945, an atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima.

show.text: 6 August 1945: Hiroshima

say.text: Around then the Soviet Union entered the war on Japan: on 8 August, or 9 August depending on the source. On 9 August a second atomic bomb hit Nagasaki, and about 40,000 people died.

show.text: 6 Aug Hiroshima | 8–9 Aug Soviet Union enters war on Japan | 9 Aug Nagasaki

say.text: These are hard numbers, so take a breath if you need one. About 80,000 died at Hiroshima at first. Counting injuries and radiation, estimates reach 90,000 to 140,000.

show.text: Hiroshima: 90,000–140,000 estimated deaths

say.text: Emperor Hirohito announced Japan's surrender on 15 August. The formal surrender was signed on 2 September 1945, which ended the war.

show.text: 15 Aug 1945 emperor announces surrender | 2 Sep 1945 formal surrender

ask.q: On what date was Japan's formal surrender signed?
ask.why: Japan's formal surrender on 2 September 1945 concluded the Pacific War. The 15 August date was the emperor's announcement.

say.text: Were the bombings justified? Historians still debate it. Defenders say the bombs avoided a costly invasion of Japan, saving lives on both sides.

show.text: Defenders: bombs ended the war and avoided invasion | Critics: see next beat

say.text: Critics, often called revisionists, argue Japan was already ready to surrender. Some say the aim was partly to impress the Soviet Union. Others raise moral objections.

show.text: Defenders: avoided invasion | Critics: Japan near surrender; other motives; moral questions

say.text: Historians also disagree about why Japan surrendered. Sadao Asada stresses the shock of the bombs. Herbert Bix argues the bombs and the Soviet declaration of war together pushed the emperor's court. Tsuyoshi Hasegawa says there's no smoking gun.

show.text: Asada: shock of the bombs | Bix: bombs plus Soviet entry | Hasegawa: no single proven cause

ask.right: Historians still disagree about why Japan surrendered
wrong: All historians agree the bombs alone ended the war
Records prove exactly which factor decided it
Historians agree Japan surrendered before 6 August
ask.why: One 2024 book on the debate says historians have reached no final resolution on the decision.

say.text: Last topic: counting the dead. Most estimates say 70 to 85 million people died, about 3 percent of the world's population.

show.text: 70–85 million deaths (estimate)

say.text: Sources do not all agree. Wikipedia's article on the war says 60 to 75 million, and its list of wars says 70 to 85 million.

show.text: Estimated total deaths, in millions

say.text: Why the gap? Many deaths went unrecorded. Also, some counts include 19 to 25 million war-related famine deaths that other compilations leave out.

show.text: Many deaths never recorded | Famine deaths counted in some lists, left out of others

ask.q: Why do estimates of World War II deaths differ?
ask.right: Many deaths went unrecorded, and sources count different kinds of deaths, such as famine
wrong: The war has no agreed end date
All estimates copy a single source
ask.why: Many deaths went unrecorded, and lists differ on whether to include famine and disease deaths.

say.text: Most of the dead were civilians. One estimate gives about 20 million military and 40 million civilians. Estimates for the Soviet Union range from about 19 to 27 million.

show.text: Military: about 20 million | Civilians: about 40 million (one estimate)

ask.q: Among the people who died in World War II, which group was the majority in most estimates?
ask.why: Most estimates say a majority of the dead were civilians.

say.text: For comparison, World War I killed an estimated 15 to 22 million people. World War II was several times deadlier.

show.text: WWI: 15–22 million | WWII: 70–85 million (one range)

say.text: Now our frame of reference: what else was going on in these years? In 1943 a Dutch doctor built the first dialysis machine in occupied Netherlands. In Britain, Colossus, an early electronic computer, reached the codebreakers at Bletchley Park.

show.text: 1943: first dialysis machine, occupied Netherlands | Dec 1943–Jan 1944: Colossus at Bletchley Park | 1945: ENIAC computer completed

say.text: Medicine moved too. By D-Day, 2.3 million doses of penicillin had been made. And these years had births. John Lennon was born in 1940. Stephen Hawking and Muhammad Ali were both born in January 1942.

show.text: June 1944: 2.3 million penicillin doses | 9 Oct 1940: John Lennon | 8 Jan 1942: Stephen Hawking | 17 Jan 1942: Muhammad Ali

ask.q: Which two famous people were both born in January 1942?
ask.why: Hawking was born on 8 January 1942 and Ali on 17 January 1942. Lennon was born in October 1940.

say.text: The big world was changing too. On 26 June 1945 the United Nations Charter was signed in San Francisco. On 26 July, Clement Attlee replaced Winston Churchill as British Prime Minister.

show.text: 26 Jun 1945 UN Charter signed | 26 Jul 1945 Attlee succeeds Churchill

say.text: To sum up: war in Europe, the Atlantic, the Soviet front, and Asia and the Pacific. It ended with Germany's surrender in May and Japan's in August and September 1945.

show.text: Europe | Atlantic | Soviet front | Pacific and Asia | Home fronts and resistance | Atomic bombs and the debate | Counting the dead

say.text: Next class is about the Holocaust: how it happened, and how the world remembers genocide. Thank you for learning with us.

show.text: Next: Class 55, The Holocaust and the Memory of Genocide

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: The musician and songwriter John Lennon is born in Liverpool, England.
Stephen Hawking is born on 8 January in Oxford, exactly 300 years after Galileo's death. Muhammad Ali is born on 17 January in Louisville, Kentucky.

Willem Kolff builds the first dialysis machine in the occupied Netherlands. The US Army contracts with the University of Pennsylvania to develop ENIAC. A British prototype of the Colossus computer is built.
The first Colossus is assembled at Bletchley Park and is working by January 1944.
Allied scientists have made 2.3 million doses of penicillin ready for the D-Day invasion.
The ENIAC computer is completed in the United States.
The United Nations Charter is signed in San Francisco. Clement Attlee succeeds Winston Churchill as British Prime Minister.

other_side.claim: World War II began on 1 September 1939 with Germany's invasion of Poland.
other_side.other_view: The National WWII Museum dates the war's beginning to 7 July 1937, when Japanese and Chinese troops clashed near Beijing and a full undeclared war followed. Which start date you pick depends on whether you count Europe or Asia first.

other_side.claim: The atomic bombs were needed to end the war and avoid a costly invasion of Japan.
other_side.other_view: Revisionist historians argue Japan was already ready to surrender and that the decision to use the bombs suggests other motives. The estimates of casualties in the planned invasion are themselves debated. A 2024 book on the debate says it has produced no final resolution.

other_side.claim: The atomic bombs caused Japan's surrender.
other_side.other_view: Some historians stress the Soviet declaration of war and invasion of Manchuria. Sadao Asada stresses the shock of the bombs, and Herbert Bix argues the bombs and the Soviet entry together convinced the emperor's court. Tsuyoshi Hasegawa says there is no smoking gun showing which mattered most. Japanese records suggest Nagasaki had little effect on decision-making.

other_side.claim: About 70 to 85 million people died in World War II.
other_side.other_view: Some tallies give lower totals, such as 60 to 75 million, or 'nearly 70 million'. Ranges differ partly because many deaths went unrecorded and partly because lists differ on whether to include famine and disease deaths.

other_side.claim: World War II was the first time American women worked outside the home in large numbers.
other_side.other_view: About a quarter of American women already worked outside the home in 1940. The war changed the type of work and how many women did it, with five million joining the workforce between 1940 and 1945.
